pedagogy.summary: This Year 5 topic builds the heliocentric model: the Sun (a star) at the centre with the planets, including Earth, orbiting it; the Moon orbiting Earth while Earth orbits the Sun; and the Sun, Earth and Moon as approximately spherical bodies. It is best taught with physical/enacted models the children move themselves, establishing sphericity explicitly and distinguishing the two nested orbits (Moon–Earth, Earth–Sun), while bridging the deep geocentric intuition using the history of ideas (Ptolemy → Copernicus).
bestPractices: Use kinesthetic/physical models children enact — be the Earth orbiting a lamp 'Sun' while a partner 'Moon' orbits you — because manipulating the model beats watching a demonstration.
Establish sphericity explicitly (the Sun, Earth and Moon are balls, not discs) using globes and real photos, since many children hold a flat-disc or flat-sky model.
Distinguish the two nested orbits clearly: the Moon orbits Earth, and Earth (with all the planets) orbits the Sun — the common confusion is what orbits what.
Bridge from the geocentric intuition to the heliocentric model using the story of ideas (Ptolemy, Alhazen, Copernicus), which makes the counter-intuitive model credible.
Handle scale honestly — flag that diagrams compress sizes and distances hugely and are not to scale.
Keep 'rotation causes day and night' as the linked next step; here concentrate on the orbital model and sphericity.
keyRepresentations: A heliocentric model — Sun-centred with the planets' orbits, Earth among them.
A nested-orbit diagram: Moon → Earth, Earth (and planets) → Sun.
Physical enactment: a child as the orbiting/spinning Earth around a lamp Sun, a partner as the Moon.
A globe plus light source, and photos showing the Sun, Earth and Moon as spheres.
A 'not to scale' caption or scale strip.
commonMisconceptions: The Sun orbits or goes around the Earth (the geocentric model), or everything orbits Earth.
The Sun, Earth and Moon are flat discs rather than spheres.
The Moon orbits the Sun directly, rather than orbiting Earth while both orbit the Sun.
The Sun is somehow different from 'a star'.
Planets are close together and similar in size (a scale error from diagrams); Pluto is still a planet.

learn.summary: Year 5 'Earth and space': build the heliocentric model — the Sun (a star) at the centre with Earth and the other planets orbiting it, the Moon orbiting Earth while Earth orbits the Sun, and the Sun, Earth and Moon as approximately spherical bodies. The core difficulty is the deep geocentric intuition and the nested two-orbit system (Moon to Earth, Earth to Sun), plus a flat-disc reading of the bodies. Teach it with enacted/physical models children move themselves, a top-down orbit model they run and compare against observation, explicit sphericity evidence, and the history of ideas (Ptolemy's Earth-centred model, Alhazen's critique of it, and Copernicus's Sun-centred model).

activities.title: Be the Earth, the Moon and the Sun — enact the nested orbits
feedback: If the Moon child drifts off to circle the lamp instead of their Earth, stop and re-tether: 'The Moon stays with its Earth — it loops you while you loop the Sun.'
If a child says the Sun moves round the Earth, ask them to name who is standing still at the centre and who is walking around whom.
Check the pair can state what orbits what before swapping roles.
activities.rationale: Upper-primary children are becoming ready for a heliocentric perspective but typically still hold a geocentric model; physically manipulating a model the child enacts is recommended, and curriculum guidance recommends using a model of the Sun and Earth. Any claim that enactment outperforms watching a demonstration is not established by the cited sources.
sourceClaims: Early-elementary children typically hold a geocentric (Earth-centred) model and struggle with sphericity and nested orbits; upper-elementary pupils become ready for a heliocentric perspective, so physical models the child manipulates are recommended.

DfE Year 5 non-statutory guidance recommends pupils learn how ideas about the solar system developed — how the geocentric model gave way to the heliocentric model via Ptolemy, Alhazen and Copernicus — and use a model of the Sun and Earth.
learnerActions: In a group of three, place a lamp or ball as the Sun. One child is the Earth and walks a slow circle around the Sun.
The 'Moon' child circles the 'Earth' child continuously WHILE the Earth keeps walking its orbit around the Sun, so both motions happen at once.
Pause and say aloud: 'The Moon goes around the Earth, and the Earth (with the Moon) goes around the Sun.'
Swap roles so every child has been the Moon that must keep looping its Earth while the Earth travels.
activities.intendedInsight: The Moon orbits Earth while the Earth–Moon pair together travel round the Sun — two simultaneous, nested orbits, not the Moon circling the Sun directly.

activities.title: Run and compare a top-down solar-system model
feedback: If the child reads the toggle as 'both are equally fine', ask them to point to what each arrangement shows for the planets' paths and which one accounts for them more simply (the Moon circles Earth in both).
If they say the Moon circles the Sun, slow the slider right down and have them trace the Moon's path relative to the Earth, not the Sun.

Note honestly that an Earth-centred picture can look like it fits everyday sunrise and sunset, so the real comparison rests on the planets' changing positions the model shows; the Moon staying with Earth happens in both arrangements, so it does not decide between them.
Reinforce: 'The Sun is at the centre; the Earth is one of the planets, and the Sun is a star.'
activities.rationale: The nested-orbit relationship and the geocentric-versus-heliocentric contrast are largely planar, so a top-down model the child runs and scrubs makes the two simultaneous motions and the comparison visible and controllable. A fixed diagram can show the layout but cannot be run or compared interactively by the learner.
sourceClaims: DfE Year 5 statutory 'Earth and space' requires pupils to describe the movement of the Earth and other planets relative to the Sun; the movement of the Moon relative to the Earth; and the Sun, Earth and Moon as approximately spherical bodies.

DfE Year 5 non-statutory guidance recommends pupils learn how ideas about the solar system developed — how the geocentric model gave way to the heliocentric model via Ptolemy, Alhazen and Copernicus — and use a model of the Sun and Earth.
learnerActions: Run a top-down view: the planets glide around the Sun while the Moon circles the Earth. Use a time slider to speed up, slow down or scrub the motion.
Watch specifically for the Moon looping the Earth AT THE SAME TIME as the Earth loops the Sun, and describe this nesting in your own words.
Flip a toggle to an Earth-centred arrangement (Sun and everything circling the Earth) and compare it with the Sun-centred one.

Compare the two using concrete things the model shows: notice that the Moon circles the Earth in both arrangements, so look at the planets. In which arrangement do the planets' paths, including times when a planet seems to drift backwards across our sky, come out more simply? Explain your choice.
activities.intendedInsight: The Sun-centred model, with the Moon still orbiting Earth, accounts for the planets' observed motions more simply; together with later observations, this is why it replaced the earlier Earth-centred model.

activities.title: Spheres, not discs — gather the evidence
feedback: If a child still describes them as circles or plates, return to a photo and the lit globe and ask what a flat disc would look like from the side.
Note that round pictures in books are flat drawings of round balls — distinguish the drawing from the body it represents.
activities.rationale: Many children hold a flat-disc or flat-sky model, so sphericity should be established explicitly with globes, photographs and observable evidence rather than assumed.
sourceClaims: DfE Year 5 statutory 'Earth and space' requires pupils to describe the movement of the Earth and other planets relative to the Sun; the movement of the Moon relative to the Earth; and the Sun, Earth and Moon as approximately spherical bodies.

Early-elementary children typically hold a geocentric (Earth-centred) model and struggle with sphericity and nested orbits; upper-elementary pupils become ready for a heliocentric perspective, so physical models the child manipulates are recommended.
learnerActions: Handle a globe lit by a single light source and describe how light falls on a ball versus a flat disc.
Look at real photographs of the Sun, Earth and Moon taken from space and state whether each is a ball or a flat circle.

List evidence that the bodies are spheres: photos from space of all three; for Earth, the curved shadow it casts on the Moon during a lunar eclipse and ships disappearing hull-first over the horizon; for the Moon, the curved edge between its lit and dark parts as its phases change.
Say the conclusion in full: 'The Sun, Earth and Moon are approximately spherical.'
activities.intendedInsight: The Sun, Earth and Moon are approximately spherical bodies, not flat discs drawn on a flat sky.

activities.title: Name and order the planets; test what-orbits-what
feedback: A matching answer that sends the Moon around the Sun shows the nesting has flattened — return to the enactment or the slowed model.
If a learner places Earth at the centre with the Sun orbiting, revisit the run-and-compare model and anchor 'the Sun is at the centre, Earth is one of the planets.'
This task checks understanding rather than teaching it: follow up wrong choices by returning to the enactment or the model, not just by marking them.
activities.rationale: Matching, ordering and a geocentric/heliocentric choice surface whether the learner coordinates the two orbits and can defend Sun-at-centre; such tasks check recall and discrimination and do not by themselves elicit the learner constructing or enacting the model.
sourceClaims: DfE Year 5 statutory 'Earth and space' requires pupils to describe the movement of the Earth and other planets relative to the Sun; the movement of the Moon relative to the Earth; and the Sun, Earth and Moon as approximately spherical bodies.
learnerActions: Name the planets in order out from the Sun and state that they all orbit the Sun.
Match each body to what it orbits: Moon to Earth; Earth and the other planets to the Sun.
Answer a geocentric-vs-heliocentric choice: which arrangement has the Sun at the centre, and why is it the accepted one?
Sort pictures or statements into 'sphere' versus 'flat disc' for the Sun, Earth and Moon.
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidate the model: Sun at the centre as a star, planets orbiting it in order, the Moon orbiting Earth, all three bodies spherical.

activities.title: Interview Copernicus — why move the Sun to the centre? (optional history companion)
feedback: If the conversation drifts into biography only, steer back to 'what does each model account for, and which does it more simply?'
Keep this as a companion to the orbit model, not a replacement for running and comparing it.
activities.rationale: The history of ideas bridges the geocentric intuition to the heliocentric model and is recommended in the non-statutory guidance; it teaches why the idea changed more than the mechanics of the model, so it supports rather than replaces the orbit work.
sourceClaims: DfE Year 5 non-statutory guidance recommends pupils learn how ideas about the solar system developed — how the geocentric model gave way to the heliocentric model via Ptolemy, Alhazen and Copernicus — and use a model of the Sun and Earth.
learnerActions: In role, or questioning a peer in role as Copernicus, ask: 'Why isn't the Earth at the centre?'
Draw out that placing the Sun at the centre accounted for the observed motions more simply than the earlier Earth-centred model.

Connect the story to the model: Ptolemy set out a detailed Earth-centred model, Alhazen (Ibn al-Haytham) criticised problems in Ptolemy's model, and Copernicus proposed putting the Sun at the centre; later observations by others helped it become accepted.
activities.intendedInsight: The counter-intuitive heliocentric model became accepted because it accounted for observations more simply and was supported by later observations (such as Galileo's telescope discoveries) — the history makes the model credible.

constraints: Core statutory goals: describe Earth and the other planets moving relative to the Sun; the Moon moving relative to the Earth; and the Sun, Earth and Moon as approximately spherical bodies.
Address the common confusions directly: the Sun orbiting the Earth (geocentric), the Moon orbiting the Sun directly (flattened nesting), and the bodies as flat discs.

Handle scale honestly: diagrams and models compress sizes and distances hugely and are not to scale — flag this with a 'not to scale' caption or scale strip rather than implying planets are close together or similar in size.
Anchor that the Sun is a star and the Earth is a planet like the others.
Keep 'rotation causes day and night' as the linked next step; here concentrate on the orbital model and sphericity.

A top-down or flat screen model represents the orbits on a plane; use rotating-globe imagery or 3D/physical balls to make clear the bodies themselves are spheres. A 3D free viewpoint can help learners feel the nesting in space but is an enhancement, not a requirement — the core orbital relationship is largely planar.

When contrasting geocentric and heliocentric arrangements, keep the comparison age-appropriate and honest: a simple Earth-centred picture can appear to fit daily sunrise/sunset, so rest the comparison on the planets' changing positions (for example, planets sometimes appearing to drift backwards across the sky), which a Sun-centred model explains more simply. Note that the Moon orbits Earth in both arrangements, so the Moon's motion alone does not decide between them. Do not claim the Earth-centred model fits nothing.

Matching, ordering and multiple-choice tasks check recognition and discrimination; they do not by themselves elicit the learner constructing or enacting the nested motions, so pair them with enactment or a runnable model.
If Pluto arises, use current convention (Pluto is a dwarf planet); do not present 'Pluto is still a planet' as correct.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
One source (IOPSpark / NSTA geocentric-model guidance) is marked verified:false in the row; treat the readiness and 'physical models the child manipulates are recommended' claims as unverified.

The original best-practice phrasing 'manipulating the model beats watching a demonstration' asserts comparative efficacy the cited sources do not establish; it has been removed from activity rationales and replaced with a recommendation to use/enact a model, qualified as unverified.

The row's framing of a static diagram as unable to teach the nested motion has been narrowed to an observable affordance/limit (a fixed diagram shows layout but cannot be run or compared interactively), not a categorical 'cannot teach' claim.

Pluto's status (the row notes 'Pluto is still a planet' as a misconception) is a classification point; present current convention that Pluto is a dwarf planet, and keep the focus on the orbital model.

The child-facing contrast between Earth-centred and Sun-centred models is simplified for Year 5. Historically, a simple geocentric view superficially matches daily sunrise/sunset and epicyclic geocentric models matched naked-eye observations fairly well; the activity has been reworded to rest the comparison on the fuller set of motions the model shows rather than implying the Earth-centred picture fits nothing.

probeDeeper: If you stood on the Moon, what would you see going around you — and what would you BOTH be going around?
How would you persuade someone who thinks the Sun goes round the Earth that it's actually the other way?
Is the Earth the centre of the solar system? If not, what is — and how do you know?
assess.correctAnswer: The Moon orbits the Earth; the Earth and the other planets orbit the Sun — so the Moon circles the Earth while the pair together travel round the Sun, which sits at the centre. The Earth is a planet like the others, and the Sun is a star.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'the Sun goes round the Earth' (geocentric model, reinforced by sunrise/sunset language)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Run a Sun-centred model beside an Earth-centred one and test which matches what we see; anchor 'the Sun is at the centre, Earth is one of the planets.'
errorPatterns.revealedBy: places the Earth at the centre with the Sun orbiting it

errorPatterns.pattern: 'the Moon orbits the Sun directly' (flattens the nested two-orbit system)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show the Moon tethered to the Earth, the Earth–Moon pair travelling together round the Sun; act it out with three children.
errorPatterns.distractor: The Moon orbits the Sun directly.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: draws or describes the Moon circling the Sun rather than the Earth

errorPatterns.pattern: 'the Sun, Earth and Moon are flat circles / discs' (2-D reading of the bodies)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Sphericity evidence — photographs from space, the round shadow Earth casts on the Moon, ships dipping below the horizon.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: describes them as circles or plates rather than balls

responseLevels.gap: Geocentric (the Sun orbits the Earth), or describes the bodies as flat; cannot say what orbits what.
responseLevels.full: Coordinates the nested system — Moon round Earth, Earth and planets round the Sun at the centre — states the Sun, Earth and Moon are spheres, and can justify heliocentric over geocentric; transfers to another planet-and-moon pair.
responseLevels.partial: Knows the planets orbit the Sun but flattens the nesting (sends the Moon round the Sun) or cannot coordinate the two simultaneous motions; states sphericity only when prompted.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Tell me the path of the Moon: what does the Moon go around, and what does THAT thing go around? … Now, how do you know the Earth travels round the Sun and not the other way?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A geocentric child puts the Earth at the centre with the Sun going round it — the reason tier surfaces this. A child who has only memorised 'planets orbit the Sun' may still send the Moon straight round the Sun, missing the nesting. Correct reasoning coordinates two simultaneous orbits and can defend Sun-at-centre.
